title: Module Header and Imports
content:
**Denumerability of the Rationals (Wiedijk #3)**

Cantor's 1874 theorem that ℚ is countable, formalized using Mathlib's `Denumerable` typeclass. The file provides the core bijection, alternative formulations (surjection, injection), explicit encode/decode functions with round-trip proofs, and the connection to cardinal arithmetic.

This is one of the most frequently formalized results across all proof assistants, and is #3 on Wiedijk's list of 100 Greatest Theorems.
mathContext: The file imports `Mathlib.Data.Rat.Denumerable` (the `Denumerable ℚ` instance), `Mathlib.Logic.Denumerable` (`Denumerable.eqv` giving `α ≃ ℕ`), `Mathlib.Logic.Equiv.Basic` (`Equiv`, `Equiv.bijective`, `Equiv.symm`), `Mathlib.SetTheory.Cardinal.Basic` (`Cardinal.mk`, `Cardinal.aleph0`, `Cardinal.mk_denumerable`), and `Mathlib.Tactic` (general tactics). The namespace is `DenumerabilityRationals` with no `open` declarations. The `/-! ... -/` docstring provides a status checklist and historical notes.

title: Mathlib's Denumerable Instance
content: The `Denumerable ℚ` instance is provided by Mathlib via `inferInstance`. This typeclass asserts that ℚ is constructively in bijection with ℕ, providing explicit encoding/decoding functions. The `example` keyword confirms Lean's typeclass resolution finds the instance automatically.
mathContext: `example : Denumerable ℚ := inferInstance` confirms that Lean's typeclass resolution can find the `Denumerable ℚ` instance from `Mathlib.Data.Rat.Denumerable`. Internally, `Denumerable α` extends `Encodable α` with the requirement that the encoding is surjective (hence a bijection). The instance for ℚ works by encoding each rational p/q (in reduced form) as a pair `(p : ℤ, q : ℕ+)` and then using the `Denumerable (ℤ × ℕ+)` instance which composes the Cantor pairing function.

title: The Explicit Bijection natEquivRat
content: `Denumerable.eqv` gives an equivalence `ℚ ≃ ℕ`. We use `.symm` to get `ℕ ≃ ℚ`, which lets us enumerate rationals by natural numbers. Internally, Mathlib's encoding represents each rational p/q in lowest terms and uses the Cantor pairing function on (numerator, denominator).
mathContext: `def natEquivRat : ℕ ≃ ℚ := (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm` extracts the concrete equivalence from the `Denumerable ℚ` instance. `Denumerable.eqv` has type `α ≃ ℕ` (from `Mathlib.Logic.Denumerable`), so `.symm` reverses it to `ℕ ≃ ℚ`. The `Equiv` type (from `Mathlib.Logic.Equiv.Basic`) bundles a forward function `toFun : ℕ → ℚ`, an inverse `invFun : ℚ → ℕ`, and proofs `left_inv` and `right_inv` certifying they are mutual inverses.

title: Cantor's Classical Statement
content: The classical formulation: there exists a bijection f : ℕ ≃ ℚ that is `Function.Bijective`. The proof extracts the equivalence from `Denumerable.eqv` and uses `Equiv.bijective` to confirm both injectivity and surjectivity. This is the existential statement closest to Cantor's original 1874 theorem.
mathContext: `theorem rationals_denumerable : ∃ f : ℕ ≃ ℚ, Function.Bijective f` is proved by `use (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm; exact (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm.bijective`. The `use` tactic provides the witness (the equivalence), then `Equiv.bijective` (which proves every `Equiv` is bijective) closes the goal. `Function.Bijective f` unfolds to `Function.Injective f ∧ Function.Surjective f`.

title: Countability Follows
content: Every denumerable type is countable (the `Countable` instance is inferred automatically). The converse is false: finite types like `Fin n` are countable but not denumerable. This illustrates Lean's typeclass hierarchy: `Denumerable → Countable → Encodable`.
mathContext: `theorem rationals_countable : Countable ℚ := inferInstance` uses the fact that `Denumerable α` implies `Countable α` via the typeclass hierarchy in Mathlib. `Countable α` means there exists an injection `α → ℕ` (but the type may be finite). The hierarchy is: `Denumerable` (bijection with ℕ, must be infinite) → `Countable` (injection into ℕ, may be finite) → `Encodable` (partial injection into ℕ).

title: Surjection ℕ → ℚ
content: Restates denumerability as the existence of a surjection from ℕ onto ℚ: every rational is the image of some natural number. This is the 'listing' perspective — the surjection provides an enumeration that hits every rational at least once.
mathContext: `theorem exists_surjection_nat_to_rat : ∃ f : ℕ → ℚ, Function.Surjective f` is proved by `use (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm; exact (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm.surjective`. The `use` tactic coerces the `Equiv` to a plain function `ℕ → ℚ` (via `Equiv.toFun`), then `Equiv.surjective` proves the surjectivity component. Note that `Function.Surjective f` unfolds to `∀ q : ℚ, ∃ n : ℕ, f n = q`.

title: Injection ℚ → ℕ
content: Restates denumerability as the existence of an injection from ℚ into ℕ: each rational receives a unique natural number label. Together with the surjection, these two theorems give the two halves of a Schroeder-Bernstein argument, though here both come from a single equivalence.
mathContext: `theorem exists_injection_rat_to_nat : ∃ f : ℚ → ℕ, Function.Injective f` uses `Denumerable.eqv ℚ` directly (without `.symm`, since the forward direction is `ℚ → ℕ`). `Equiv.injective` proves the injectivity. `Function.Injective f` unfolds to `∀ q₁ q₂ : ℚ, f q₁ = f q₂ → q₁ = q₂`.

title: Encode/Decode Functions and Round-Trip Proofs
content:
**encodeRatToNat** wraps `Denumerable.eqv ℚ` and **decodeNatToRat** wraps its `.symm`. Two round-trip theorems certify they are mutual inverses:
- `decode_encode`: encoding then decoding recovers the rational
- `encode_decode`: decoding then encoding recovers the natural number

Both are proved by `simp`, which unfolds definitions and applies `Equiv.symm_apply_apply` / `Equiv.apply_symm_apply`.
mathContext: `def decodeNatToRat (n : ℕ) : ℚ := (Denumerable.eqv ℚ).symm n` and `def encodeRatToNat (q : ℚ) : ℕ := Denumerable.eqv ℚ q` are thin wrappers around the equivalence. `theorem decode_encode (q : ℚ) : decodeNatToRat (encodeRatToNat q) = q` is proved by `simp [decodeNatToRat, encodeRatToNat]`, which unfolds both definitions and applies `Equiv.symm_apply_apply` (the left-inverse law). `theorem encode_decode (n : ℕ) : encodeRatToNat (decodeNatToRat n) = n` similarly applies `Equiv.apply_symm_apply` (the right-inverse law).

title: Rationals are Infinite
content: Confirms the `Infinite ℚ` instance via `inferInstance`. This is a prerequisite for denumerability — a type is denumerable iff it is both countable and infinite. Finite types are countable but not denumerable.
mathContext: `theorem rationals_infinite : Infinite ℚ := inferInstance` confirms typeclass resolution finds the `Infinite ℚ` instance. `Infinite α` (from `Mathlib`) asserts that the type has no finite upper bound on cardinality. For ℚ, this follows from the injection `ℕ → ℚ` given by `Nat.cast`. A type is `Denumerable` iff it is both `Countable` and `Infinite`.

title: Cardinal Equality: |ℚ| = ℵ₀
content: Proves `Cardinal.mk ℚ = Cardinal.aleph0` using `Cardinal.mk_denumerable`. This bridges the type-theoretic perspective (Denumerable typeclass) with the set-theoretic perspective (cardinal arithmetic). The one-line proof shows the deep integration between Mathlib's typeclass and cardinal systems.
mathContext: `theorem card_rat_eq_aleph0 : Cardinal.mk ℚ = Cardinal.aleph0 := Cardinal.mk_denumerable ℚ` applies the lemma `Cardinal.mk_denumerable` (from `Mathlib.SetTheory.Cardinal.Basic`) which states that for any `[Denumerable α]`, `Cardinal.mk α = Cardinal.aleph0`. `Cardinal.mk α` computes the cardinality of type `α` as a `Cardinal` value. `Cardinal.aleph0` is ℵ₀, the smallest infinite cardinal.

title: Cardinal Equality: |ℚ| = |ℕ|
content: Proves that ℚ and ℕ have the same cardinality by rewriting both sides to ℵ₀. This is the set-theoretic restatement of Cantor's original theorem: the rationals and naturals are equinumerous despite the rationals being dense and the naturals being discrete.
mathContext: `theorem card_rat_eq_card_nat : Cardinal.mk ℚ = Cardinal.mk ℕ` is proved by `rw [card_rat_eq_aleph0, Cardinal.mk_denumerable ℕ]`. The `rw` tactic rewrites the left side using `card_rat_eq_aleph0` (proved above) to get `Cardinal.aleph0 = Cardinal.mk ℕ`, then rewrites the right side using `Cardinal.mk_denumerable ℕ` to get `Cardinal.aleph0 = Cardinal.aleph0`, which closes by reflexivity.
